extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students researching standards for preliminary injunctions and the evidentiary weight of prior judgments
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evidentiary standards governing when courts will grant preliminary (provisional) injunctions in patent litigation, with emphasis on the weight to be given to prior judgments, Patent Office actions, interferences, and public acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of a judgment depends on mode of decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of a judgment in the Circuit court depends to some extent upon the mode in which its conclusions were attained. A decree based upon a hearing, in which all questions of fact as well as of law were submitted to the judge and by him were examined and decided, is of greater weight than one based on the verdict of a jury on a feigned issue, or than a judgment on a verdict in a court of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/citations given (e.g., Fisher, Buchanan). A hearing before a master is not a final hearing. A decision on a motion for a preliminary injunction is of less weight than a final decree. Courts should consider how thoroughly questions were examined when assessing prior judgments for injunction motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of decree by consent and collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree by consent, if without collusion, binds the defendant in the same circuit, but has no effect on other parties, nor against him in other circuits, unless his first surrender is shown to have resulted from his knowledge that he had no adequate defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collusive decrees are of no value against any party. A decree by consent in one circuit does not lay foundation for an injunction in another. Where present device differs only in form from that concerning which defendant consented to a decree, an injunction may nevertheless issue. Collusion in a former suit must be fully proved, not conjectured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weight: preliminary injunction decisions vs final decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision on an application for a preliminary injunction is of less weight than a final decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decision on a motion for a preliminary injunction is not controlling authority in another circuit; verdicts sustaining a patent may relieve a court of the need to inquire into validity when granting provisional relief, but a final decree carries more weight. Courts may decline injunctions where the judgment relied on has been appealed and seems doubtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge conclusions vs jury verdicts for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusions of a judge on a patent case are more reliable than those of a jury; the verdict of a jury is not conclusive on a motion for an injunction, though the court will examine the whole case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge in equity may examine evidence and draw his own conclusions when deciding an injunction, but should be cautious about substituting his view for a jury's where the jury acted within its province. Historical cases (Day v. Hartshorn, Wells v. Gill) illustrate limits on setting aside jury verdicts for injunction purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office decisions: persuasive but not binding; weight depends on contest and examination
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision in the Patent Office, though not binding on the courts, has more or less weight according to the subject-matter of the judgment, and the violence of the contest by which it was preceded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An award of a patent without objection is not sufficient alone to empower a court to interfere for protection of its owner. A Patent Office decision after long contest and full examination is of weight on a motion for an injunction. Construction given to a patent in the Patent Office will generally be followed in courts. But Patent Office actions are not controlling when validity is actively contested in the courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of re-issue and allowance errors on injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of the Patent Office in allowing a re-issue is of weight on a motion for an injunction, but a re-issue granted to correct a mistake made by an attorney in accepting an amended claim is of too doubtful validity to aid an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Amheim v. Finster and similar examples. Courts weigh the reason and circumstances of re-issue when deciding whether to credit it for injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference judgments: priority vs validity
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference judgment awarding priority to one rival claimant is sufficient ground for an injunction in his favor against the other as to priority, but an interference decision affects only the matter of priority and is not evidence of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An interference decision raises a presumption against the defeated party and may warrant injunctions, especially if the defeated party had knowledge of the prior art or acted in bad faith. If an interference judgment is appealed, it is not operative as a judgment for injunction purposes; if not appealed it is strongly persuasive. Interference rulings as to identity of inventions are relied on by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive force of judgments by higher tribunals or same circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment of the Supreme Court, or of the Circuit court of the same circuit, upon the same issues and against the same defendant, is conclusive proof of the validity of the patent, unless new evidence has since been discovered or the judgment has been overruled or was originally obtained by fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments in other circuits are not conclusive but are of high authority and can be overcome only by convincing evidence that the tribunal was mistaken or insufficiently informed. A decision by the Commissioner of Patents is not conclusive as to novelty, utility, or inventive skill, but may have prima facie value.

rubrics_metrics.name: No judgment is conclusive against non-parties or non-privities
rubrics_metrics.description: No judgment is conclusive against persons who were neither parties nor privies to the suit; but where certain questions of law relating to the existence, scope, or validity of the patent have been once decided after full examination, these decisions command respect in other courts and causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decision rendered by the Supreme Court or the same Circuit court is not departed from without clear evidence of error. Prior judgments that are not estoppels leave the issue open for fresh inquiry on an injunction motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending appeals/writs of error diminish weight of prior judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment is not conclusive on a motion for an injunction if a writ of error is pending; the court may refuse an injunction where the judgment on which it was asked has been appealed from and seems doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Wells v. Gill, Many v. Sizer). Courts will normally exercise independent judgment when an appeal is pending and may deny provisional relief until finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgments declaring invalidity are powerful evidence against a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments against the patent are, for obvious reasons, of higher value and a wider influence, since a patent invalid upon any ground is invalid against all the world, and therefore any decision declaring it void, though in a different tribunal and between other parties, affords a presumption of its invalidity which the plaintiff can with difficulty overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conflicting judgments exist, courts tend to follow those of higher authority; a judgment of invalidity in the Federal courts is conclusive on the parties. Multiple defeats at law without public acquiescence ordinarily lead to denial of injunction absent a clear case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of conflicting judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: When conflicting judgments have been rendered, the court must follow those which, in view of all the tests of authority, appear to have the higher value, and if the question is still doubtful, and no other evidence is offered, it must decide in favor of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh authority, completeness of examination, and reliability of earlier tribunals when reconciling conflicts; absent better reasons, prior decisions that examined questions fully will command respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acquiescence as substitute evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no judgment sustaining the patent can be offered, or where such judgment is of doubtful value, the deficiency may be supplied by proof of a public acquiescence in the claims of the patent of sufficient definiteness and duration to afford a reasonable presumption of its validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquiescence is a voluntary submission, against interest, to an asserted right. Proofs include exclusive possession and exercise of the right after grant (manufacture, repeated sales, licensing), long undisputed use with public acquiescence, acceptance by the public, and use/sale prior to application. Such evidence can justify a provisional injunction even if some doubt of validity remains; special facts may, however, take a case out of the general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acceptance and use before patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: The use and sale of the invention by the plaintiff before he applied for a patent, and the acquiescence of the public in his exclusive claims, is to be regarded as evidence of patentability and of recognition of the plaintiff's claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider acceptance by the public and long undisputed use as important indicia. Sufficient acquiescence will support injunctive relief even where the patent has not been finally adjudicated valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of verdicts in uncontested cases and pro forma decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: A verdict in an uncontested case, without collusion, is of as great weight as one after a full trial; a decree pro forma on the merits is not ground for an injunction in other courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncontested verdicts may be treated as authoritative for injunction motions. Pro forma decrees or consent decrees entered without a hearing carry little weight in other tribunals.
